thread.title_full: We miss Pathmark and the grocery wars that once ruled New Jersey - NewsBreak

author: David M. Zimmer
title: We miss Pathmark and the grocery wars that once ruled New Jersey - NewsBreak
text:
By David M. Zimmer ,
18 hours ago
In November 1968, North Jersey shoppers opened their newspapers to find an announcement from a familiar supermarket executive.
“I used to be president of Shop-Rite,” Herb Brody told customers in a two-page advertisement introducing a new name: Pathmark.
Stores in Clifton, Passaic, Hackensack and dozens of other communities were getting new signs. But the change was more than a rebranding. It was one of the most consequential supermarket breakups in New Jersey history.
It marked a bitter split within Wakefern Food Corp. that nearly crippled the cooperative, created one of New Jersey's biggest supermarket rivals and reshaped the region's grocery business for decades.
Brody, then a vice chairman of Supermarkets General Corp., was helping introduce Pathmark to customers at 43 supermarkets in northern New Jersey.
Story continues below photo gallery.
The Record called the conversion a “merchandising metamorphosis.” Behind it was a dispute over expansion and voting power within Wakefern Food Corp., the cooperative that supplied independently owned ShopRites.
The separation cost Wakefern nearly half its wholesale business and established a rival that would spend decades competing for New Jersey shoppers.
Supermarket split in New Jersey The split developed in 1966 as Supermarkets Operating Co. of Cranford and General Supermarkets Inc. of Passaic prepared to merge. The companies together operated 64 ShopRites during the merger dispute, according to contemporary coverage in The Record.
Their combined company, Supermarkets General, would have enough stock to elect nine of Wakefern’s 18 directors, according to a federal appeals court opinion recounting the dispute. Other directors adopted a resolution requiring the company to leave.
Supermarkets General sued. A settlement rescinded the attempt, expanded Wakefern’s board to 20 directors and required 12 affirmative votes for board action. The additional seats went to a class of shareholders outside the merging companies’ group.
Story continues below photo gallery.
Expansion presented another source of friction, recalled Allen Bildner, whose family founded Kings Super Markets, in a 2008 oral history recorded by Rutgers University. A Wakefern membership committee reviewed proposed locations with the interests of existing members in mind.
“They were not permitted to just take any location,” Bildner said.
By January 1968, Supermarkets General operated 78 ShopRites and was negotiating its departure, according to The Record. An agreement in April 1968 terminated its stockholdings and membership in Wakefern. The company would initially remain a wholesale customer but had to relinquish the ShopRite name, label and merchandising program.
That November, company President Milton Perlmutter described the separation as a move to gain “greater flexibility to serve the public.”
Supermarkets General had recently completed a 500,000-square-foot grocery warehouse in Woodbridge. Two computers would handle the routing of merchandise to its stores, Perlmutter told reporters at a press conference preceding the name change.
The Record reported annual sales exceeding $550 million and holdings that included 83 supermarkets, nine Pathmark gas stations, 11 Crown Pathmark drugstores and 22 Genung’s department stores. The Pathmark name was already being used on the company’s gas stations and drugstores before it appeared on the supermarkets.
For the remaining Wakefern members, the loss threatened the wholesale operation they shared. Supermarkets General accounted for 49% of its volume when it announced its departure in 1966, U.S. Bankruptcy Judge Raymond T. Lyons wrote in a 2001 opinion examining the cooperative’s history. Completing the withdrawal took two years.
“The cooperative barely survived,” Lyons wrote.
Bildner’s oral history put the recovery of the lost volume at about three years. ShopRite and Pathmark became major competitors in a market also served by A&P, Grand Union, Food Fair, Acme and other chains.
“Price was god,” he recalled.
Groceries after midnight Pathmark gave shoppers another reason to try its stores: They could go when much of the competition was closed.
A June 14, 1972, advertisement in Connecticut’s Manchester Evening Herald featured testimonials from overnight customers. One shopper, identified as Jo Ann Sobalsky, described going at 1 a.m. and finishing in 20 minutes instead of an hour and a half. She and her husband worked nights.
Other testimonials featured customers shopping after work or a night out. Store schedules varied with local regulations, particularly on Sundays, and the longer hours sometimes brought objections from neighbors.
In Belleville, officials were debating late shopping at the Belmont Avenue Pathmark by June 1972. Company representatives argued that the hours accommodated shift workers and households with two working spouses, according to coverage in the Belleville Times.
The issue resurfaced in 1981, when complaints from Silver Lake residents prompted the company to voluntarily limit the store’s hours while officials considered restrictions on late-night businesses.
In 1974, a Pathmark in South Plainfield became an early testing site for barcode scanning. Few products arrived with the codes printed on their packaging, leaving employees with the task of producing and attaching about 250,000 labels a week, project participant Bill Daley recalled in a 2012 account for Supermarket News.
Night crews helped label the merchandise. The system that promised to simplify checkout first required workers to put codes on thousands of products by hand.
Equipment breakdowns and shortages sometimes meant early morning trips to Newark Airport to collect emergency shipments of labels. Supermarket executives visited South Plainfield to watch the checkout equipment operate.
Pathmark changes hands In October 1987, an investor group led by Merrill Lynch Capital Partners Inc. and Supermarkets General executives took the company private in a leveraged buyout, financing the acquisition with debt the business would have to repay.
In later Securities and Exchange Commission filings, company officials attributed Pathmark’s 2000 bankruptcy to debt and interest costs associated with the buyout, while describing the underlying supermarket operation as sound.
Pathmark and its parent companies filed for Chapter 11 protection on July 12, 2000. When the company emerged on Sept. 19, about $1 billion in subordinated debt had been canceled.
Bildner later called the Merrill Lynch transaction “the beginning of the end for Pathmark.”
Investment in the stores continued after the restructuring. In 2003, then-CEO Eileen Scott told Supermarket News that, as of the end of 2002, 82% of Pathmark’s supermarkets had been built or renovated during the previous five years. The company completed 24 renovations in 2001 and nine in 2002.
In December 2007, A&P completed its acquisition of Pathmark, bringing 141 stores into the Montvale-based company. The approximately $1.4 billion transaction was financed through cash, equity and about $475 million in borrowing, according to A&P’s later bankruptcy disclosures.
A&P, founded in 1859 in New York City, filed for bankruptcy in December 2010, emerged in March 2012 and filed again in July 2015. The second proceeding led to store sales and closings across the region. By Thanksgiving 2015, the last A&P-owned stores had closed and the original Pathmark chain had ceased operating.
The Pathmark trademark found a buyer. Allegiance Retail Services, the New Jersey company associated with Foodtown and other supermarket banners, acquired the brand in 2016. On May 1, 2026, a former Foodtown in East Meadow, New York, opened as Pathmark Daily, according to the trade publication Mass Market Retailers.
Allegiance is a cooperative of independent supermarket owners. Nearly six decades after Supermarkets General’s departure from Wakefern, the Pathmark name belongs to another cooperative.
Supermarkets in New Jersey today The era when ShopRite, Pathmark and A&P towered over New Jersey's grocery business has given way to a more crowded marketplace. The major supermarket chains that operate in New Jersey today include ShopRite, Acme Markets, Aldi, Stop & Shop, Wegmans, Whole Foods Markets, Trader Joe's, Kings Food Markets, Key Foods and Lidl. Groceries are also sold at Walmart and Target locations.
This article originally appeared on NorthJersey.com: We miss Pathmark and the grocery wars that once ruled New Jersey
